Game teardown · 07:04 · 50 markers reviewed

For The Fame

selected

An autobattler in which the main skill happens before combat: buy, position, and connect items so that the resulting grid can win on its own.

3×3 inventory × item synergies × three room choices × autobattle
DeveloperLuc Francey / lf-games studio
Release16 August 2026
Platformsitch.io; also GX.games and Kongregate
AIitch.io states that generative AI was not used

Why Radar selected it

5,000+plays in the first week · developer report
18 · 4.6/5itch.io ratings at the time of review
71comments, including poison/bleed builds and win streaks

The signal is not based on one large number. Players on itch.io discuss specific builds and 15–17 consecutive wins; on 29 August, the developer shipped a balance patch addressing the poison meta and unfair builds. That is evidence that players reached systemic mastery and that the developer is already responding to an emerging meta.

Counterpoint. YouTube does not explain the distribution: an external IndieBunny video had 38 views, 3 likes, and 0 comments, and remained at 38 views from 1 to 15 September. The meaningful signal is concentrated on game platforms and in player discussion.
itch.io5,000+ devlogGX.gamesbalance patchYouTube snapshot

Rules and core loop

1Choose one of three rooms
2Buy, receive, or upgrade an item
3Place it in the 3×3 grid
4Watch two builds autobattle
5Gain a trophy or lose a heart

The built-in rules state the goal with unusual precision: build the strongest item grid, win 10 trophies, choose between a shop, event, or bonus three times, fight an opponent, and do not die. The recorded run began with five hearts. Two early losses reduced the reserve to three, after which three victories produced 3/10 trophies.

Each item occupies one cell and combines several layers: price, primary stat, cooldown, active and passive effects, and keywords. Position matters because some effects reference adjacency or another item. The player does not control attacks directly; the autobattle tests the quality of the prior decisions.

Controls: the mouse selects rooms, buys and places items, opens tooltips, and advances to the next stage. Combat has no direct input; the player observes triggers and can inspect both grids.

Observed room types

  • Damage and Non-Damage shops
  • Bank and Gift Room
  • Fountain and direct currency/regen bonuses
  • Text events with a choice
  • Room ninety-nine with storage
  • Fight another crawler

What reads well

Each decision is compact

Most screens request one action: choose a room, buy an item, take a free reward, or begin combat. The navigation stays contained despite the system's depth.

The stakes remain visible

Hearts, trophies, and currency stay on the left; the route to the next fight stays above. Every victory or loss immediately changes a legible run resource.

Builds are comparable

Both grids remain visible during combat and on the result. This creates material for discussion: what triggered, which item cycled faster, and where block or poison changed the outcome.

Reference material is embedded

Rules, Items, and Keywords explain the system without sending the player to an external page. A large effect vocabulary needs this layer.

Where the system loses causality

The autobattle shows damage and triggers, but quickly becomes a stream of small numbers. The result screen says Victory or Defeat without identifying the main cause: which item dealt the most damage, what blocked most often, which synergy stayed idle, or why. A new player understands the outcome but not always the next correction.

  • Heal
  • Block
  • Regen
  • Bleed
  • Poison
  • Rush
  • Slow
  • Stun
  • Charge

Transfer

Turn a build result into a portable artefact: grid, key synergy, trophy count, and a short combat summary on one card.

Avoid

Do not force players to diagnose a fast autobattle from floating numbers alone. Report item contribution and inactive connections.

Experiment

After combat, show three lines: top damage source, best defensive item, and one unused synergy. Compare rearrangement rate and starts of the next fight.

Reason to return

The next version of the player's grid, not merely the next level. Player comments show that a language of builds has already formed.

Screen-by-screen product anatomy

Interface specification

A reconstruction-oriented inventory of the visible hierarchy, controls, states, interruptions, and feedback in For The Fame. It describes observed recording evidence first; recommendations are explicitly labelled.

Evidence convention. Observed means the state is visible in the reviewed session or captured UI. Implementation guidance marks a production requirement inferred from the interaction model, not a claim about unseen code.

Viewport map

Run status header

Coins, hearts, trophies, and run progress persist across rooms at the top edge; each value is paired with an icon and readable current state.

Room decision stage

Most non-combat rooms use three centered choice cards. Combat replaces them with two opposing 3×3 item boards while preserving the top run context.

Reference and outcome layer

Item/keyword tooltips, rules glossary, utility-room decisions, battle resolution, and victory/defeat use overlays that pause or gate the next room.

Overlays & interruptions

  • Mode-selection explanation and three-card room map/choice states.
  • Shop and utility-room purchase/choice sheets.
  • Item tooltips plus tabbed Rules / Items / Keywords reference.
  • Battle victory/defeat, trophy/heart consequence, and 10-trophy run-win results.

Motion, VFX & feedback

  • Item cooldown fills/rings and activation pulses establish automatic-combat causality.
  • Damage, block, healing, and status applications use source-to-target motion plus signed numbers.
  • Drag-valid slots glow; invalid destinations reject and snap the item back.
  • Coin, heart, and trophy changes travel to the persistent header and receive distinct audio/visual weight.
  • Victory burst, defeat tint/shake, and room-card transition are brief enough to preserve run cadence.

Responsive, accessibility & edge cases

  • Every drag action needs click-to-select and keyboard alternatives; every hover tooltip needs focus/tap persistence.
  • Do not encode friendly/enemy or positive/negative states solely with hue; use side labels, icons, signs, and motion.
  • On narrow screens, stack the two battle boards vertically or provide a stable scaled layout without changing slot order.
  • Persist after each resolved room and purchase, not mid-animation; restore to a deterministic completed state.
Reconstruction test. A player must choose a mode and room, buy and position an item, inspect every keyword, watch an auto-battle and explain its trigger order, resolve a utility trade, and understand exactly how hearts, coins, trophies, and the 10-trophy run target changed.

Creator context · verified public sources

Developer dossier

Who made For The Fame, the public context around the work, and the nearest verified projects. Private identity, location, employment, and credits are left unknown unless the creator or an official project page states them.

Public identity and credit

For The Fame is made by Luc Francey, who publishes games as LF and uses @francey_luc. His public profile describes him as building For The Fame and links the browser prototype with its planned Steam product.

Location and working context

Francey’s public X profile lists Bulle, Switzerland. This is creator-provided profile information. The reviewed sources do not establish a studio headcount; official store credits should remain the authority if the commercial build adds collaborators.

Timeline

The public browser prototype launched on itch.io around 16–17 August 2026. The page labels it a prototype, links later-platform ambitions, and declares no generative AI; ongoing public posts show interface and explanation work after release.

Other verified work

Francey’s official itch profile lists One Man Factory (factory automation through cloning), Anormaly, and Defuse the Bomb Simulator. It also surfaces Digital Kingdom-related titles, but those are not attributed to Francey alone without explicit project credits.

Visible development pattern

The verified solo catalog favors compact, legible system toys and prototypes. For The Fame pushes that tendency into a larger auto-battler run structure with position-sensitive inventory, keywords, room economy, and a clear 10-trophy objective.

What this means for the teardown

The creator’s other prototypes support the importance of transparent rules and automation feedback. For reconstruction, preserve explainability—tooltips, cooldown cause/effect, room exchange—and do not copy profile-adjacent team titles into an individual portfolio.

Identity boundary. Name and location are used because the developer publishes them. Related creators or Digital Kingdom pages visible on itch are not treated as proof of sole authorship.

04
Reconstruction blueprint

What must exist to rebuild the observed game

This is a product and systems specification derived from the public build and the recorded first session. It describes observable behaviour, not the original source-code architecture.

Reconstruction confidence. High for the first-run structure, room cadence, board rules, combat presentation, and primary run stakes. Medium for the complete item pool, opponent-selection logic, and late-run meta.

State machineSession flow

  • Mode select → Practice or Normal Dungeon.
  • Room draft → choose one of three shop, event, bonus, utility, or combat destinations.
  • Board edit → buy or receive an item, inspect its tooltip, and place it into one of nine cells.
  • Autobattle → both grids execute cooldown-driven effects without direct player input.
  • Result → award one trophy on victory or remove one heart on defeat, then return to the route.
  • Terminal state → ten trophies wins the run; exhausting the five-heart reserve ends it.

Input contractControls

  • Mouse selects rooms, purchases items, moves them between cells, opens tooltips, and advances screens.
  • Combat is observational: no attack or dodge input was exposed during the recording.
  • Rules, Items, and Keywords panels act as the in-product reference layer.

Rules engineSimulation and resolution

  • The inventory is a fixed 3×3 grid; one item occupies one cell.
  • Items combine cost, a primary statistic, cooldown, active behaviour, passive behaviour, and keywords.
  • Some effects inspect adjacency, another item, or a combat condition, so position changes output.
  • Health belongs to the combat instance; hearts and trophies belong to the run.
  • Three non-combat room choices precede the next opponent in the observed cadence.
  • Floating numbers communicate execution, but a faithful rebuild also needs per-item combat accounting for diagnosis.

Meta layerEconomy and progression

  • Coins are spent in specialised shops; gifts, fountains, banks, events, and bonuses alter the economy without combat.
  • The build grows horizontally through more items and vertically through upgrades or stronger effects.
  • Hearts provide loss tolerance, while trophies expose distance to the ten-win run goal.
  • Opponent builds function as both difficulty and social proof: the player compares two complete grids after every fight.

Required screen and interface inventory

Mode selection and run start
Three-way room-choice map
Damage / non-damage shop
Event, fountain, bank, gift, and bonus rooms
3×3 board editor with item tooltips and storage
Side-by-side autobattle
Victory / defeat result
Rules, item catalogue, and keyword glossary

Minimum useful data model

  • ItemDefinition: id, name, price, icon, base stat, cooldown, targeting rule, active effect, passive effect, keywords, upgrade path.
  • BoardState: nine ordered slots plus optional storage; placement changes neighbour queries.
  • RunState: coins, hearts, trophies, room cycle, current inventory, visited events, difficulty seed.
  • CombatState: two boards, health pools, effect timers, status stacks, deterministic event log, result summary.
  • RoomDefinition: category, offer generator, price rules, reward or choice payload, continuation route.

06
Production sequence

Build the causal loop before the content surface

A practical implementation order for reproducing the observed promise while keeping the prototype testable at every step.

  1. Implement a deterministic two-board simulator with health, cooldowns, damage, block, and an event log.
  2. Add the 3×3 editor and two adjacency-sensitive items; prove that moving one cell changes the outcome.
  3. Add the room cadence, coins, hearts, trophies, and a ten-trophy terminal condition.
  4. Expand the keyword/effect registry, shops, events, upgrades, and opponent archetypes from data.
  5. Finish with combat contribution summaries, seeded balance tests, save/resume, and shareable build cards.

Boundaries and unresolved behaviour

Do not encode these as facts yet.
  • Exact stacking and ordering rules for simultaneous effects were not exhaustively tested.
  • How Normal Dungeon sources opponents, scales difficulty, or handles asynchronous player builds remains unverified.
  • The complete item catalogue, rarity model, storage restrictions, and post-win progression lie outside the recording.
